newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT - AUSSIE DOLLAR CONTINUES MODEST RECOVERY.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - AUSSIE DOLLAR CONTINUES MODEST RECOVERY.

text.p: AUS$ S/Term range *Support *Restnce *RSI-14 *MA-10 *MA-20
*Offshore range roughly US$0.7360/7390
*Australian dollar continues to move away from last Friday's two year lows under U$0.73.
*The dollar seen hving potential to edge higher, with resistance expected from US$0.7400
*Aussie improves on crosses as U.S. dollar firms overnight
*RBA governor Macfarlane to speak in Perth later on Tuesday
The Australian dollar continued its modest recovery from last Friday's two-year lows, putting on another quarter of a cent in overnight trade and edging towards a test of US$0.7400.
The gains followed the half cent gains made in offshore trade on Friday, and continued the recent pattern of large moves in the dollar offshore followed by a more subdued local trading session.
By 8.00 a.m. (2200 GMT) the dollar was at US$0.7383/88, below its overnight high but still up on the US$0.7362/67 level it was at in late trade on Monday.
Dollar sentiment was helped by a further rise in the price of gold, arising from nervousness about U.S. stocks and bonds.
With the unit having found some support, traders said the unit could continue to edge higher, although solid resistance was expected on moves to US$0.7400.
On the downside, the dollar has also now created a buffer above the US$0.7295 level hit last Friday.
While the dollar could test lower again, with US$0.7330 a potential target, it was not seen to be as vulnerable to testing fresh two year lows as it had been over the last two days.
The dollar also improved on the crosses after the U.S. dollar reclaimed some of Friday's losses, helped by a steadying performance on Monday in U.S. asset markets after Friday's sell-off.
The Australian dollar opened at 85.74/84 yen and 1.3754/67 marks from a local close on Monday of 84.72/82 and 1.3588/3605.

The market is waiting on a speech by Reserve Bank of Australia governor Ian Macfarlane in Perth at a dinner later today (11.00 p.m./1300 GMT), his first public appearance since the last rate cut and the RBA's decision to sell two thirds of its gold reserves.
His speech, entitled "Monetary policy and Growth", will be examined by markets for evidence of the RBA's current thinking on the economy and therefore the likelihood of another cut in interest rates.
However, because of time differences between Sydney and Perth, the speech, will not hit the screens until well after the local market's close.
-- John Mair, Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
